title: Grandeur in this view
hook: Darwin ends the Origin: there is grandeur in this view of life

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Muir and the mountains. Your line was nature's peace will flow into you. Did you find the farthest thing you could see? Today, a naturalist kneels, in words at least, beside a weedy bank. Day one thousand twenty-four.

A bank of earth, overgrown. Weeds tangled together, birds in the bushes, insects in the air, worms working in the wet soil. Nobody would put it on a postcard. But it's the picture Charles Darwin chose for the last paragraph of On the Origin of Species: "It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth". From that muddy bank, he builds to his final sentence. And its key word is grandeur.
screen: `AN OVERGROWN BANK.` → `NOT A POSTCARD.` → `HIS LAST PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: Here is how the book ends: "There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved." Four things to hear. First, the entangled bank. Darwin's awe doesn't start with a mountain or a galaxy. It starts with weeds and worms, ordinary life, crowded together in the dirt. Second, grandeur. It's a word for size and splendor, the kind people use for palaces and mountains. Darwin spends it on weeds and worms, and on the long process that made them. Third, two clocks at once. The planet goes "cycling on" by a fixed law, round and round. Meanwhile life does something else entirely: it branches, from a simple beginning into "endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful." One steady circle, one endless unfolding. Fourth, the tense. "Have been, and are being, evolved." Not finished. Still happening, on the bank, in the garden, now. People read this sentence in very different ways. Some people of faith hear in it the wonder of creation still at work. Some people with no faith at all hear wonder enough in the process itself. Darwin's sentence makes room for both readers. And both can stand on the same muddy bank and say the same word.
screen: `AN ENTANGLED BANK` · `GRANDEUR FOR WEEDS AND WORMS` · `FROM SO SIMPLE A BEGINNING` · `STILL BEING EVOLVED` · then, large: `GRANDEUR IN THIS VIEW.`

segments.voice: The practice is to look at a living thing's design. A leaf, a houseplant, an insect on the window, a pet, or your own hand. Choose one, and look at how it's put together. Where it branches. Where it joins. How one part fits another. Don't name the parts. Just follow them with your eyes, slowly, the way you'd follow a path. When your attention drifts, come back to the next joint, the next curve. The bell holds the time.
Entangled bank. Darwin's image for ordinary life, weeds and worms, from which he saw grandeur: life branching, from so simple a beginning, into endless forms. Today's word.
Your line: endless forms most beautiful. Find one tangled, overlooked patch of life today, a weedy corner, a crack in a wall, and give it a full look. Day one thousand twenty-four.

howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path, religious and not, read the last paragraph of the Origin as a meditation on life, and practice slow, close looking at living things in gardens, parks and overgrown corners.

trapdoor: what you thought: grandeur is a word for palaces.
what it means: Darwin's word for awe at life branching from a simple beginning into endless forms.

what a scholar hears: the sentence sets two motions side by side, a planet "cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity" and life unfolding into "endless forms most beautiful", and keeps it in the present tense.

'whilst' is Darwin's spelling inside the quotation.
